Learning from Fleet Experience: Collective Experience Learning across 96 Robots

∷ Collective Experience Learning
Paper Code

01

CEL: learning from a fleet’s own experience

As robots carry out tasks, they collect real-world experience that can help robot foundation models improve during deployment. Larger fleets collect this experience in parallel, potentially accelerating policy improvement. One way to realize this potential is to learn from human corrections. However, this requires experts to monitor execution and provide corrective actions when robots need help. The demand for expert supervision increases as fleets grow. Human supervision thus becomes a bottleneck: robots can gather experience at increasing scale, but their ability to learn from it remains constrained by the availability of experts.

We introduce Collective Experience Learning (CEL), a paradigm in which robots share experience generated during deployment to improve a common policy. The figure above shows how the source of actions used for learning changes: human demonstrations in SFT, expert interventions in (M)HG-DAgger, and successful robot executions in the CEL workflow shown here. After expert-supervised initialization, CEL pools the fleet’s experience and returns updated policies to the robots. One robot’s successful actions can then help improve the policy used by others, without additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. In our implementation, humans provide outcome labels and reset environments.

For phone packaging, a long, multi-stage industrial task, the policy’s success rate increased from 79.2% to 98.3% in evaluations on two robots of the same model that had not collected training data. Over 120 trials per policy, failures fell from 25 to 2, a 92% reduction. The benefits of scale are also evident: with collection time per robot held fixed, increasing the training fleet from 16 to 96 robots raised success from 86.7% to 98.3%. More robots translated into more reliable task execution.

Putting CEL into practice requires overcoming two challenges. First, how can robots find useful experience in large collections of trajectories with only binary success-or-failure labels? Second, how can a large robot fleet keep collecting experience despite limited communication bandwidth and local faults?

02

FERT: using failures to find what worked

As robots carry out tasks, CEL gathers a growing pool of experience across the fleet. A task can run for several minutes and span thousands of timesteps, yet its final outcome supplies just one label: success (1) or failure (0). The challenge is to turn this sparse feedback into effective training. We developed Failure-guided Experience Retrieval Fine-Tuning (FERT) to organize fleet-generated experience for retrieval and policy fine-tuning. Successful trajectories enter a shared experience buffer. Observations preceding a failure serve as queries to find similar successful segments, matching visual features and joint state over time. The actions in these segments supply the training targets, and the segments are sampled more often during fine-tuning. A success recorded by one robot can therefore help others learn from situations where they struggled.

03

From folding a T-shirt to packing a phone

We used five tasks to test how learning from shared experience helps robots handle flexible objects, control contact and use tools. Each task has its own policy, trained on dual-arm AgiBot G2 robots.

04

Five real-world tasks: how much does collective experience help?

We evaluated FERT on five real-world manipulation tasks: flower arrangement, clothes folding, phone charging, stool assembly and phone packaging. FERT outperformed all baselines and human operators across all five tasks. Multi-robot (M)HG-DAgger raised mean success across the five tasks from 36.3% to 81.0%, providing stronger starting policies for further learning. Without additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions, FERT then raised mean success to 97.3%, a gain of 16.3 percentage points and an 86.0% reduction in mean failure rate. On phone charging, success increased from 60.0% to 97.5%, reducing failures by 93.8%. On phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raised success from 79.2% to 98.3%, reducing failures by 92.0%. These results show that FERT can improve the reliability of initialized policies through collective experience under the evaluated tasks and training configurations. We tested each policy on two AgiBot G2 robots that had not collected training data, with 60 trials per robot and no human intervention. The charts below show success rates over these 120 trials per task, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals.

Scaling trends emerge in online robot training

To see how performance changes as more robots contribute, we varied fleet size while keeping collection time per robot fixed. Across the five tasks, FERT generally improves with larger fleets. On phone packaging, success reaches 50.8%, 86.7% and 98.3% with 4, 16 and 96 training robots, respectively. The 4-robot result falls below the starting policy’s 79.2%, while expanding from 16 to 96 robots adds 11.7 percentage points. By collecting autonomous experience with solely binary task-outcome labels, FERT provides a practical route to expanding the experience available for policy improvement. Dashed lines mark the SFT and (M)HG-DAgger starting policies.

Ablation study: What makes the learning loop work?

To understand how each part of the learning loop contributes, we ran an ablation study on phone packaging, testing four design choices with 16 training robots and 120 evaluation trials per configuration. The full configuration reaches 86.7% success. Removing the 30 frames of context on either side of each retrieved segment, while keeping retrieval, lowers it to 57.5%. Both choosing relevant examples and keeping the surrounding movements matter for learning the sequence. We also varied how often robots receive updated policies and how much previous sampling priority carries forward. Among the settings we tested, synchronizing every 500 optimizer steps and retaining 88% of previous priorities each gave the highest success rate.

05

FATS: Learning together without waiting for everyone

Collective experience learning turns a robot fleet into a distributed training system. Keeping that system stable is a challenge: robots may go offline, edge nodes may lose their connections, and some robots may pause for resets or recovery. To keep these local interruptions from holding up the whole learning process, we developed the Fault-tolerant Asynchronous Training System (FATS). Asynchronous collection and fault recovery allow available robots to continue contributing experience while recovered workers rejoin the fleet, helping collective learning continue through interruptions.

HotSwarm: a robot hot-plugging system

To keep training data consistent through interruptions, HotSwarm gives each restarted worker a new identity. When a robot’s control process fails, it restarts the process at the same workstation and rebuilds its connections. The other robots keep collecting. The incomplete episode is discarded, and the replacement rejects late actions addressed to its predecessor. If an inference worker fails, it restarts and reloads the current policy. If training workers fail, they resume from a saved checkpoint. During training recovery, surviving cloud inference workers continue serving their current policy, while new experience waits in the channels until training resumes. Operators handle scene resets and hardware repairs.

SwarmLink: connecting robots and training

Cloud inference and fleet learning share the same network link, so bulk data transfers must leave room for robots waiting for actions. SwarmLink pools incoming observations for available cloud inference workers, which batch requests and return actions to the corresponding robots. Meanwhile, execution records and task outcomes stream to a cloud trajectory collector. The collector combines them with observations and policy outputs already available in the cloud, avoiding a second upload of those observations. It releases an episode to training only when all required fields and the outcome are present. Interaction traffic takes priority over bulk transfers, allowing collection and learning to overlap.

System performance: keeping collection running

In a 96-robot run, the fleet collected 9,834 episodes despite 30 fault incidents affecting 22 robots. The recorded faults cost 1.3% of the fleet’s total robot time. Local recovery also changes how robot faults scale: adding robots increases the number of faults, while each recovery still interrupts only the affected workers. Under the same per-robot fault rates and downtime, the model keeps the fraction of time available for collection steady as the fleet grows.

06

Conclusion

We introduce Collective Experience Learning (CEL), a paradigm in which robots improve a shared policy during deployment using fleet-generated experience after expert-supervised initialization. We realize CEL through Failure-guided Experience Retrieval Fine-Tuning (FERT), which uses successful executions as action supervision and failures to select relevant successful experience. A Fault-tolerant Asynchronous Training System (FATS) supports this learning process by coordinating robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization despite interruptions to individual robots. Together, these components enable the fleet to supply experience for subsequent policy updates without additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieved 93.3–99.2% success on robots excluded from training data collection.
